config.title: Unnecessary Re-renders

intro.title: Unnecessary Re-renders
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React app that demonstrates how components can re-render unnecessarily, even when their props or state haven't changed. You will learn to identify these wasteful updates by using the browser's developer tools. The core concept involves understanding React's rendering behavior and how to optimize performance by preventing these extra renders. You'll work with functional components, state hooks, and props to see the issue in action.
intro.usecase: Unnecessary re-renders are a common performance issue in data-rich React applications like financial dashboards or e-commerce product filters. For example, in a dashboard displaying multiple live charts, updating one metric shouldn't cause all other charts to re-render, wasting CPU cycles and slowing the UI. Similarly, in a large form with many input fields, typing in one field shouldn't trigger re-renders for unrelated sections, which can cause noticeable lag for users. Learning to identify and prevent these re-renders is essential for building smooth, professional-grade interfaces that scale efficiently.

objectives: Identify components that trigger unnecessary re-renders in a React application
Apply React.memo to prevent re-renders of functional components with unchanged props
Configure useMemo to cache expensive calculations and avoid recomputation on every render
Implement useCallback to memoize event handlers and prevent unnecessary child component updates
Update component structures to lift state up and reduce prop drilling that causes re-renders
Construct custom hooks that optimize performance by controlling side effect dependencies
Manipulate dependency arrays in useEffect to prevent excessive effect executions

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in both React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in the component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty div element for now.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function. Make sure to return a JSX element.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns an empty div.
successCriteria: A functional component named App exists and returns an empty div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the component is named exactly 'App' and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a function named App that returns a div element.

steps.title: Initialize state for a counter
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'count' initialized to 0.
steps.hint: Call useState(0) and destructure the returned array into [count, setCount].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a state variable
const [score, setScore] = useState(100);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a 'count' state variable ready to track numeric values.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with initial value 0, and the state variable is named 'count'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with 0 as the initial value and naming the variable 'count'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState(0) to create a state variable named 'count' inside the App component.

steps.title: Initialize state for a toggle
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to create a state variable named 'isOn' initialized to false.
steps.hint: Add a second useState call similar to the count state, but with the variable name 'isOn' and initial value false.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a toggle state
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: count and isOn.
successCriteria: The component contains a state variable 'isOn' initialized to false using useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created a state variable named 'isOn' with an initial value of false.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState to create a state variable named 'isOn' with an initial value of false.

steps.title: Create handler for incrementing counter
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function named incrementCounter that increases the count state by 1.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses setCount to update the state. You can use the previous state value to calculate the new count.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an incrementCounter function that updates the count state when called.
successCriteria: The incrementCounter function is defined inside the component and uses setCount to increase count by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it correctly updates the count state by 1. Check that you're using setCount properly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The incrementCounter function is missing or doesn't update the count state correctly. Review how to update state in React.

steps.title: Add a console.log to track renders
steps.instruction: Add a console.log statement at the top of your App component's body to log 'App rendered' each time the component renders.
steps.hint: Place console.log('App rendered'); right after the opening curly brace of your component function, before any state declarations.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will log 'App rendered' to the console each time it re-renders, helping you visualize when renders occur.
successCriteria: console.log('App rendered') is placed at the top of the App component body, before any state declarations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the console.log is placed at the very top of the component body, before any state declarations.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding console.log('App rendered'); right after the opening curly brace of your App component function.

steps.title: Display the counter value
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your component, add a paragraph element that displays the current count value.
steps.hint:
Use JSX to render a

tag with the count state variable inside curly braces.
steps.analogousExample:
// Display a value in JSX

Current value: {someState}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current count value in a paragraph element.
successCriteria: A paragraph element is added to the return statement that displays the count state variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're displaying the count variable inside a paragraph element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element displaying the count value is missing or incorrect.

steps.title: Add increment button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Increment' inside the fragment. Set its onClick handler to call the incrementCounter function.
steps.hint: Place the button after the paragraph that displays the count. Use the onClick prop and pass the incrementCounter function reference.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with an event handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Increment' appears in the UI. Clicking it will increase the counter value displayed in the paragraph.
successCriteria: A button element with text 'Increment' is added to the fragment. The button's onClick prop is set to incrementCounter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it has the correct text and the onClick handler is properly wired to incrementCounter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not correctly connected. Check that you added a button element with text 'Increment' and onClick={incrementCounter}.

steps.title: Display the toggle state
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element inside the fragment that displays 'Toggle is: ' followed by the current value of the isOn state.
steps.hint: Use JSX curly braces to embed the isOn value in the paragraph text.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a state value in JSX

Current status: {isActive}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show a paragraph displaying the current toggle state value (true/false).
successCriteria: A paragraph element with the text 'Toggle is: ' followed by the isOn state value is added to the fragment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a paragraph, but make sure it displays 'Toggle is: ' followed by the isOn value using curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph displaying the toggle state is missing or incorrect. Add a paragraph that shows 'Toggle is: {isOn}'.

steps.title: Add toggle button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button with the text 'Toggle' inside the component's return statement, and wire its onClick event to the toggleHandler function.
steps.hint: Place the button JSX after the existing paragraph and increment button. Use the onClick prop with the handler function name.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with click handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A 'Toggle' button appears in the UI that toggles the isOn state when clicked.
successCriteria: The button element with text 'Toggle' is present in the return statement, and its onClick prop calls toggleHandler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but check that it has the correct text 'Toggle' and the onClick prop is wired to toggleHandler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle button is missing or not properly connected. Add a <button> with text 'Toggle' and onClick={toggleHandler}.

steps.title: Observe unnecessary re-renders in console
steps.instruction: Add a console.log statement inside your component to track when it re-renders.
steps.hint: Place console.log('App rendered') at the beginning of your component function, before the state declarations.
steps.expectedOutcome: After adding the console.log, you'll be able to see in the browser console that clicking either button causes the component to re-render, even when only one state value changes.
successCriteria: The component contains a console.log statement that logs a message when the component renders.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to add console.log('App rendered') at the beginning of your component function, before the state declarations.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding console.log('App rendered') inside your component function, right after the opening curly brace of the App function.
